claim: DkTx is a tarantula toxin isolated from the venom of a Chinese bird spider.
source: Double-knot toxin (DkTx) is a tarantula toxin isolated from the venom of a Chinese bird spider (Bae et al., 2012; Bohlen et al., 2010) that activates the transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) channel.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Bae et al., 2012; Bohlen et al., 2010) that reported the isolation and characterization of DkTx.

claim: DkTx activates the TRPV1 channel.
source: Double-knot toxin (DkTx) is a tarantula toxin isolated from the venom of a Chinese bird spider (Bae et al., 2012; Bohlen et al., 2010) that activates the transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) channel.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Bae et al., 2012; Bohlen et al., 2010) that demonstrated DkTx activation of TRPV1.

claim: TRPV1 is a cation channel expressed in nociceptive sensory neurons.
source: TRPV1 is a cation channel expressed in nociceptive sensory neurons that plays important roles in the transduction of noxious stimuli as well as thermosensation (Julius, 2013), but the molecular mechanism of heat-dependent activation has remained elusive.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Julius, 2013, which is a review on TRPV1 function.

claim: TRPV1 plays important roles in the transduction of noxious stimuli and thermosensation.
source: TRPV1 is a cation channel expressed in nociceptive sensory neurons that plays important roles in the transduction of noxious stimuli as well as thermosensation (Julius, 2013), but the molecular mechanism of heat-dependent activation has remained elusive.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Julius, 2013, which reviews the physiological roles of TRPV1.

claim: DkTx has an unusual bivalent architecture comprised of two inhibitor-cysteine-knot (ICK) motifs designated as K1 and K2 lobes.
source: From a structural perspective, DkTx is intriguing because it has an unusual bivalent architecture, being comprised of two inhibitor-cysteine-knot (ICK) motifs that have been designated as the K1 and K2 lobes.
evidence: The claim is based on the structural characterization of DkTx described in the manuscript.

claim: DkTx is quite hydrophobic and requires the use of detergents to efficiently fold in vitro.
source: DkTx is also quite hydrophobic, requiring the use of detergents to efficiently fold in vitro (Bae et al., 2012), which raises the possibility that the toxin might interact with TRPV1 in a membrane environment, similar to toxins targeting voltage-sensing domains of voltage-activated ion channels.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bae et al., 2012, which reported the folding requirements of DkTx.

claim: Near-atomic resolution structures of the TRPV1 channel were solved using single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), including a closed state (apo), a capsaicin-bound state, and an open state with both DkTx and RTx bound.
source: In a recent breakthrough, near-atomic resolution structures of the TRPV1 channel were solved using single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), including a closed state (apo), a capsaicin-bound state, and an open state with both DkTx and the vanilloid resiniferatoxin (RTx) bound (Cao et al., 2013; Liao et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cao et al., 2013 and Liao et al., 2013, which reported the cryo-EM structures of TRPV1.

claim: The structure of the TRPV1/DkTx/RTx complex reveals that the DkTx lobes bind to sites at the periphery of the external pore of the channel.
source: The structure of the complex between TRPV1 and DkTx/RTx unambiguously reveals that the DkTx lobes bind to sites at the periphery of the external pore of the channel.
evidence: The claim is based on the structural analysis of the TRPV1-DkTx complex from cryo-EM data.

claim: The resolution of electron density maps was insufficient to reveal the structure of DkTx in atomic detail in the published TRPV1/DkTx/RTx complex structure.
source: However, the resolution of electron density maps was insufficient to reveal the structure of DkTx in atomic detail.
evidence: The claim is based on the assessment of the quality of the cryo-EM density maps in the published structures.

claim: The two lobes K1 and K2 of DkTx can fold independently.
source: Because previous studies have demonstrated that the two lobes (or knots) of the toxin, K1 and K2, can fold independently and can also activate the TRPV1 channel (Bae et al., 2012; Bohlen et al., 2010), we synthesized K1 and K2 individually using solid-phase peptide synthesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bae et al., 2012 and Bohlen et al., 2010, which demonstrated independent folding of K1 and K2.

claim: K1 and K2 can activate the TRPV1 channel independently.
source: Because previous studies have demonstrated that the two lobes (or knots) of the toxin, K1 and K2, can fold independently and can also activate the TRPV1 channel (Bae et al., 2012; Bohlen et al., 2010), we synthesized K1 and K2 individually using solid-phase peptide synthesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bae et al., 2012 and Bohlen et al., 2010, which showed that K1 and K2 can activate TRPV1.

claim: The backbone proton chemical shift values of DkTx are nearly identical to those measured for K1 and K2 separately, except for a few residues in the linker region and in the N- and C-termini.
source: The backbone proton chemical shift values of DkTx were found to be nearly identical to those measured for K1 and K2 separately, except for a few residues in the linker region and in the N- and C-termini of the toxin (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The structures of isolated K1 and K2 are highly similar to those in full-length DkTx.
source: We can therefore conclude that the structures of isolated K1 and K2 are highly similar to those in full-length DkTx.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the NMR chemical shift comparison between isolated K1/K2 and full-length DkTx.

claim: Each lobe of DkTx consists of two anti-parallel beta-strands stabilized by three disulfide bonds.
source: Each lobe consists of two anti-parallel beta-strands (F21-Y22/K32-K33 in K1 and L61-D62/Y70-C71 in K2), stabilized by three disulfide bonds.
evidence: The claim is based on the NMR structure determination of K1 and K2.

claim: The backbone root mean square deviation (RMSD) of the NMR structures of K1 and K2 relative to the average is 0.4 Å for the most ordered regions.
source: The backbone root mean square deviation (RMSD) of the structures in these ensembles relative to the average is 0.4 Å for both K1 and K2 (for the most ordered regions of each protein, which include Cys2-Cys31 in K1 and Cys44-Cys71 in K2).
evidence: The claim is based on the statistical analysis of the NMR structure ensembles.

claim: The fold of K1 and K2 is similar but not identical, with a backbone RMSD of 1.45 Å for the core 28 residues.
source: Comparison of the structures of K1 and K2 reveals that their fold is similar, but not identical; the root mean square difference (RMSD) in their backbone, for the core 28 residues, is 1.45 Å (1.56 Å including all heavy-atoms).
evidence: The claim is based on structural comparison of the NMR structures of K1 and K2.

claim: Two notable differences between K1 and K2 are the length of loop 3 and the configuration of a tryptophan side-chain in loop 2.
source: Two notable differences between K1 and K2 are the length of loop 3, which is longer in K1 than in K2, and the configuration of a tryptophan side-chain in loop 2 (W11 in K1 and W53 in K2), which is more solvent accessible in K1 (154 ± 16 Å2) than in K2 (132 ± 7 Å2).
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of the NMR structures of K1 and K2.

claim: Both K1 and K2 feature a large cluster of exposed hydrophobic residues.
source: Surface renderings of K1 and K2 show that both lobes feature a large cluster of exposed hydrophobic residues (green), comprised of W11, M25, F27 and I28 in K1 and W53, L65, A66, F67 and I68 in K2 (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by surface rendering analysis shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: The hydrophobic surfaces in both K1 and K2 are surrounded by basic and acidic residues.
source: The hydrophobic surfaces in both K1 and K2 are surrounded by basic residues (blue) and acidic residues (red), including D1, E7, K13, K14, H30 and K32 in K1 and E47, E49, K56, E72, K73 and R75 in K2.
evidence: The claim is based on surface rendering analysis of the NMR structures.

claim: The amphipathic character of DkTx is reminiscent of voltage-sensor toxins such as hanatoxin, SGTx1, VSTx1 and GxTx-1E.
source: This pronounced amphipathic character is reminiscent of well-characterized voltage-sensor toxins such as hanatoxin (Takahashi et al., 2000), SGTx1 (Lee et al., 2004), VSTx1 (Jung et al., 2005) and GxTx-1E (Lee et al., 2010), which interact with voltage-sensing domains of Kv channels within a membrane environment (Gupta et al., 2015; Lee and MacKinnon, 2004; Milescu et al., 2009; Milescu et al., 2007; Phillips et al., 2005b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on voltage-sensor toxins and their membrane interactions.

claim: The published structural models of TRPV1 (PDB entries 3J5Q and 3J5P) show a significant number of stereochemical violations and steric overlaps.
source: Aside from the missing backbone fragments and side-chains in unresolved regions, the published structural models show a significant number of stereochemical violations and steric overlaps (Tables 1, 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by the evaluation metrics presented in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: The MolProbity score ranks PDB entries 3J5Q and 3J5P in the 29th and 36th percentile, respectively.
source: As an example, the MolProbity score, which is a standardized metric of model quality among structures of comparable resolution, ranks PDB entries 3J5Q and 3J5P in the 29th and 36th percentile, respectively (with 100th percentile being the best score).
evidence: The claim is based on MolProbity analysis of the published TRPV1 structures.

claim: The published model of the TRPV1/DkTx/RTx complex is based on a map with imposed fourfold symmetry, despite the fact that the two DkTx lobes are not identical.
source: A specific issue pertaining to the published model of the TRPV1/DkTx/RTx complex is that it is based on a map with imposed fourfold symmetry, despite the fact that the two DkTx lobes are not identical and thus the appropriate symmetry for the complex would be twofold.
evidence: The claim is based on the analysis of the symmetry used in the published cryo-EM structure.

claim: In the published structure of the TRPV1/DkTx/RTx complex, the toxin is modeled as a poly-alanine chain based on the structure of hanatoxin.
source: More importantly, in the published structure of the TRPV1/DkTx/RTx complex, the toxin is modeled as a poly-alanine chain based on the structure of hanatoxin because an atomic-resolution structure of DkTx had not yet been solved.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the modeling approach used in the published structure.

claim: The improved ROSETTA models of apo TRPV1 and the TRPV1-DkTx complex have MolProbity scores that rank in the 92nd and 80th percentile, respectively.
source: To tackle these methodological issues, we used the molecular-modeling software suite ROSETTA (Leaver-Fay et al., 2011) (see Methods). This approach enabled us to develop atomic models of apo TRPV1 and the TRPV1-DkTx complex that are considerably improved; the updated MolProbity scores rank these complete models in the 92nd and 80th percentile, respectively, while maintaining the original quality of the fit to the experimental cryo-EM maps (Tables 1, 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by the MolProbity scores presented in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: DkTx binds to the outer pore of TRPV1 in a counter-clockwise (CCW) configuration.
source: Analysis of these two ensembles shows that the majority of the 100 CCW models fit to the experimental cryo-EM map significantly better, and also have a better ROSETTA score, than the majority of the 100 CW models (Figure 2E). This result is consistent with the observation that the number of NOE-restraint violations in the CW initial seed model generated with Xplor-NIH was twice as large as for the CCW model, for a comparable fit quality (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). We can therefore conclude unambiguously that DkTx binds to the outer pore of TRPV1 in a CCW configuration (Figure 2B,D,F; Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROSETTA modeling and NOE restraint analysis shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: K1 and K2 engage the outer pore of TRPV1 using loop 2 and loop 4.
source: The model of the TRPV1-DkTx complex reveals that K1 and K2 engage the outer pore of TRPV1 using loop 2 and loop 4 (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is based on the structural model of the TRPV1-DkTx complex shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Loop 2 of DkTx caps the S6 helix from one TRPV1 subunit, while loop 4 localizes near the N-terminus of the re-entrant pore helix from the adjacent subunit.
source: These two loops straddle the interface between TRPV1 subunits, with loop 2 capping the S6 helix from one subunit, while loop 4 localizes near the N-terminus of the re-entrant pore helix from the adjacent subunit.
evidence: The claim is based on the structural model of the TRPV1-DkTx complex.

claim: Mutations I599A, F649A, A657P, and F659A in TRPV1 disrupt activation of the channel by DkTx.
source: Scanning mutagenesis previously identified four residues within the outer pore domain of TRPV1, namely I599A at the top of S5, F649A in the pore loop, and both A657P and F659A at the top of S6, where mutations disrupt activation of the channel by DkTx (Bohlen et al., 2010); two additional mutants in this region (V595A in S5, and T650A in the pore loop) also display diminished activation by the toxin, whereas Y631A, near the N-terminus of the pore helix, enhances the effect of DkTx.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bohlen et al., 2010, which reported the mutagenesis results.

claim: Mutations V595A and T650A in TRPV1 display diminished activation by DkTx.
source: Scanning mutagenesis previously identified four residues within the outer pore domain of TRPV1, namely I599A at the top of S5, F649A in the pore loop, and both A657P and F659A at the top of S6, where mutations disrupt activation of the channel by DkTx (Bohlen et al., 2010); two additional mutants in this region (V595A in S5, and T650A in the pore loop) also display diminished activation by the toxin, whereas Y631A, near the N-terminus of the pore helix, enhances the effect of DkTx.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bohlen et al., 2010, which reported the mutagenesis results.

claim: The Y631A mutation in TRPV1 enhances the effect of DkTx.
source: Scanning mutagenesis previously identified four residues within the outer pore domain of TRPV1, namely I599A at the top of S5, F649A in the pore loop, and both A657P and F659A at the top of S6, where mutations disrupt activation of the channel by DkTx (Bohlen et al., 2010); two additional mutants in this region (V595A in S5, and T650A in the pore loop) also display diminished activation by the toxin, whereas Y631A, near the N-terminus of the pore helix, enhances the effect of DkTx.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bohlen et al., 2010, which reported the mutagenesis results.

claim: Among the TRPV1 residues where mutations affect DkTx activation, only F649, A657, T650 and Y631 could interact directly with the toxin according to the structural model.
source: Our model indicates that among these residues, only F649, A657, T650 and Y631 could interact directly with the toxin, suggesting that the other mutations influence toxin activation of the channel through an indirect mechanism (see below).
evidence: The claim is based on the structural model of the TRPV1-DkTx complex.

claim: Both K1 and K2 drape over the top of S6 at the presumed interface with the surrounding membrane and position several conserved hydrophobic residues where they would interact directly with lipids in the bilayer.
source: Interestingly, the model also shows that both K1 and K2 drape over the top of S6 at the presumed interface with the surrounding membrane, and position several conserved hydrophobic residues (W11, F27 and I28 in K1, and W53, F67 and I68 in K2) where they would interact directly with lipids in the bilayer.
evidence: The claim is based on the structural model of the TRPV1-DkTx complex.

claim: 1 µM K1K1 produced comparable activation to that produced by the same concentration of DkTx or K2K2.
source: Indeed, we found that 1 µM K1K1 produced comparable activation to that produced by the same concentration of DkTx or K2K2 (Figure 3C,D), suggesting that the efficacy of the two knots is comparable, but that the affinity of K1 is much lower than that of K2.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The efficacy of K1 and K2 for activating TRPV1 is comparable, but the affinity of K1 is much lower than that of K2.
source: Indeed, we found that 1 µM K1K1 produced comparable activation to that produced by the same concentration of DkTx or K2K2 (Figure 3C,D), suggesting that the efficacy of the two knots is comparable, but that the affinity of K1 is much lower than that of K2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the electrophysiological data comparing K1K1, K2K2, and DkTx.

claim: Both DkTx and K2K2 exhibited slow dissociation, while K1K1 showed considerably more rapid dissociation.
source: Although both DkTx and K2K2 exhibited slow dissociation, we observed considerably more rapid dissociation for K1K1 (Figure 3C), confirming that K1 has lower binding affinity than K2 even when tested in its bivalent form.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: K1 has lower binding affinity than K2 even when tested in its bivalent form.
source: Although both DkTx and K2K2 exhibited slow dissociation, we observed considerably more rapid dissociation for K1K1 (Figure 3C), confirming that K1 has lower binding affinity than K2 even when tested in its bivalent form.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the dissociation kinetics data for K1K1 and K2K2.

claim: Chimeras in which loop 2, loop 4 or the C-terminal part of K2 were transferred into K1-ΔL exhibited considerably more robust activation compared to K1-ΔL.
source: In contrast, chimeras in which loop 2, loop 4 or the C-terminal part of K2 were transferred into K1-ΔL [i.e. K1(K2L2), K1(K2L4) or K1(K2CT)] exhibited considerably more robust activation compared to K1-ΔL (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The weak activation observed with K1-ΔL was not altered in constructs in which either Asn1 in the N-terminus or loop 3 of K2 were transferred into K1-ΔL.
source: The weak activation observed with K1-ΔL (Figure 3F; green) was not altered in constructs in which either Asn1 in the N-terminus or loop 3 of K2 were transferred into K1-ΔL [i.e. K1(D1N) or K1(K2L3)] (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The gain of function observed with loop 2 and loop 4 transfer supports the notion that these two loops engage directly with the outer pore of TRPV1.
source: The negative results observed with the N-terminal mutant and the loop 3 transfer, together with the gain of function observed with loop 2 and loop 4 transfer, support the notion that these two loops engage directly with the outer pore of TRPV1, as observed in our model (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the chimera functional data and the structural model.

claim: The C-termini of K1 and K2 are likely to interact with the pore turret (residues 604–626) of TRPV1.
source: The model also provides a possible explanation for the gain of function observed when the C-terminus of K2 is transferred to K1. The location of the C-termini of K1 and K2 indicates that they are likely to interact with the pore turret (residues 604–626) of TRPV1 (Figure 3G), a region absent in our model as it was deleted from the TRPV1 construct used for cryo-EM (Liao et al., 2013), but preserved in the full-length construct used for our functional studies.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural model and the gain of function observed with the C-terminal chimera.

claim: Two regions of the extracellular surface of TRPV1 form the most persistent side-chain contacts with either of the two lobes of DkTx: the N-terminus of the pore-helix (primarily via Y631) and a stretch of the pore-loop and N-terminus of S6 (including N652, D654, F655, K656, A657 and V658).
source: Two regions of the extracellular surface of the channel stand out as forming the most persistent side-chain contacts with either of the two lobes of DkTx, namely the N-terminus of the pore-helix, primarily via Y631, and a stretch of the pore-loop and N-terminus of S6, including N652, D654, F655, K656, A657 and V658; additional interactions are mediated by K535 and E536, in S4 (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Video 2).
evidence: The claim is based on MD simulation analysis shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Additional interactions between DkTx and TRPV1 are mediated by K535 and E536 in S4.
source: Two regions of the extracellular surface of the channel stand out as forming the most persistent side-chain contacts with either of the two lobes of DkTx, namely the N-terminus of the pore-helix, primarily via Y631, and a stretch of the pore-loop and N-terminus of S6, including N652, D654, F655, K656, A657 and V658; additional interactions are mediated by K535 and E536, in S4 (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Video 2).
evidence: The claim is based on MD simulation analysis shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Many of the contacts on the toxin are with residues that are equivalent in K1 and K2, including W11 and W53, F27 and F67, K14 and K56, and G12 and G54.
source: Many of the contacts on the toxin are with residues that are equivalent in K1 and K2, e.g. W11 and W53, F27 and F67, K14 and K56 and G12 and G54, respectively, and a computational alanine-scanning (Ala-scan) analysis of the toxin-channel interface, based on the configurations explored during the MD simulation (see Methods), indicate that these are all influential (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on MD simulation analysis and computational alanine-scanning shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Computational alanine-scanning indicates that W11/W53, F27/F67, K14/K56, and G12/G54 are all influential in the toxin-channel interaction.
source: Many of the contacts on the toxin are with residues that are equivalent in K1 and K2, e.g. W11 and W53, F27 and F67, K14 and K56 and G12 and G54, respectively, and a computational alanine-scanning (Ala-scan) analysis of the toxin-channel interface, based on the configurations explored during the MD simulation (see Methods), indicate that these are all influential (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on computational alanine-scanning analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The most interesting unique interactions for K2 involve S55, L65, and R75.
source: The most interesting unique interactions for K2 involve S55 (K13 in K1), L65 (M25 in K1) and R75 (K35 in K1).
evidence: The claim is based on MD simulation analysis of the toxin-channel interface.

claim: S55, L65, and R75 in K2 are located in loop 2, loop 4, or the C-terminus, and transfer of these segments from K2 into K1 yields a pronounced increase in the binding affinity of isolated K1.
source: The persistence of these interactions is worth noting because these residues are located in either loop 2 (S55), loop 4 (L65) or the C-terminus (R75), and transfer of these segments from K2 into K1 yields a pronounced increase in the binding affinity of isolated K1 (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is based on MD simulation analysis and functional data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: S55, L65, and R75 in K2 are predicted to have a significant stabilizing effect by computational alanine-scanning.
source: These residues are also predicted to have a significant stabilizing effect by the computational Ala-scan (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on computational alanine-scanning analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The MD simulation reveals that interactions between DkTx and the membrane occur concurrently with those with the channel.
source: Interestingly, the simulation of the TRPV1-DkTx complex also reveals that interactions between toxin and the membrane occur concurrently with those with the channel (Figure 4B,C,E).
evidence: The claim is based on MD simulation analysis shown in Figure 4B,C,E.

claim: Several hydrophobic residues in loop 2 and loop 4 of both K1 and K2 form long-lived interactions with lipids, including W11, F27 and I28 in K1, and W53, F67 and I68 in K2.
source: Several hydrophobic residues in loop 2 and loop 4 of both K1 and K2 stand out as forming long-lived interactions with lipids, including W11, F27 and I28 in K1, and W53, F67 and I68 in K2.
evidence: The claim is based on MD simulation analysis of toxin-lipid interactions.

claim: Both K1 and K2 showed some unique interactions with lipid head-groups, for example Y70 (in K2) and H30 (in K1).
source: Both knots also showed some unique interactions with lipid head-groups, for example Y70 (in K2) and H30 (in K1) (Figure 4B,C,E).
evidence: The claim is based on MD simulation analysis shown in Figure 4B,C,E.

claim: DkTx partitions into membranes with a mole-fraction partition coefficient (Kx) of (2.3 ± 0.7) × 10^6.
source: To quantify the extent of partitioning as a function of lipid concentration, we measured the relative fluorescence intensity in a blue-shifted region of the spectra (e.g. 320 nm) as a function of lipid concentration, and fit a partition function to the data to obtain a mole-fraction partition coefficient (Kx) of (2.3 ± 0.7) × 106, indicating an energetically favorable interaction of DkTx with lipid membranes (Figure 5A, right).
evidence: The claim is based on tryptophan fluorescence spectroscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The strong interaction of DkTx with membranes would facilitate binding of the toxin to the channel by increasing the local concentration of the toxin near the channel and by a reduction in the dimensionality of diffusion within the membrane.
source: This strong interaction of DkTx with membranes would facilitate binding of the toxin to the channel by increasing the local concentration of the toxin near the channel and by a reduction in the dimensionality of diffusion within the membrane (Axelrod and Wang, 1994).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the membrane partitioning data and supported by a citation to Axelrod and Wang, 1994.

claim: K1 exhibits stronger membrane partitioning than K2, with Kx values of (3.9 ± 1.1) × 10^5 for K1 and (2.0 ± 0.2) × 10^4 for K2.
source: We conducted similar experiments for K1 and K2 separately, and observed that both K1 and K2 exhibit blue shifts upon addition of LUVs, although interestingly the blue shift of K2 was considerably smaller compared to K1 (Figure 5B,C). Fitting of a partition function to the data yielded Kx values of (3.9 ± 1.1) × 105 for K1 and (2.0 ± 0.2) × 104 for K2, suggesting that the interaction of K1 with lipid membranes is stronger compared to K2.
evidence: The claim is based on tryptophan fluorescence spectroscopy data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: Both K1K1 and K2K2 showed increased Kx values compared to K1 and K2, respectively, with K1K1 exhibiting a higher Kx value than K2K2.
source: Indeed, both K1K1 ([2.9 ± 0.3] × 106) and K2K2 ([8.1 ± 2] × 104) showed increased Kx values compared to K1 and K2, respectively, and K1K1 exhibited a higher Kx value when compared to K2K2, confirming that partitioning of K1 into membranes is more favorable than K2.
evidence: The claim is based on tryptophan fluorescence spectroscopy data for K1K1 and K2K2.

claim: Partitioning of DkTx into membranes would be disproportionately mediated by K1, leaving K2 available to engage TRPV1 and initiate formation of the toxin-channel complex.
source: These results are remarkable when considering that K2 has a higher affinity for TRPV1 compared to K1, leading us to propose a model whereby partitioning of DkTx into membranes would be disproportionately mediated by K1, leaving K2 available to engage TRPV1 and initiate formation of the toxin-channel complex (see Discussion).
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the differential membrane partitioning and channel binding affinities of K1 and K2.

claim: The measured free energies of membrane partitioning for DkTx, K1K1, and K2K2 reveal a systematic energetic penalty for bivalency between 4.8 to 6.3 kcal mol−1.
source: Although bivalency in DkTx clearly plays an important role in channel activation, it also increases the local concentration of the two lobes relative to each other and may promote interactions between the two. Indeed, the measured free energies of membrane partitioning (ΔG° = −RT lnKx) for DkTx (ΔG° = −8.5 kcal mol−1), K1K1 (ΔG° = −8.7 kcal mol−1) and K2K2 (ΔG° = −6.6 kcal mol−1) reveal a systematic energetic penalty for bivalency between 4.8 to 6.3 kcal mol−1 if we calculate the theoretical free energies for bivalent toxins (DkTx ΔG° = −13.3 kcal mol−1; K1-K1 ΔG° = −15 kcal mol−1; K2-K2 ΔG° = −11.6 kcal mol−1) from that measured for the monovalent toxins (K1 ΔG° = −7.5 kcal mol−1; K2 ΔG° = −5.8 kcal mol−1) assuming complete additivity of the free energies for partitioning of each lobe.
evidence: The claim is based on thermodynamic analysis of the membrane partitioning data.

claim: A version of DkTx with a highly flexible linker comprised of 7 Gly residues (7G-DkTx) has a Kx value indistinguishable from wild-type DkTx.
source: To test this possibility we constructed a version of DkTx wherein the linker was replaced with a highly flexible linker comprised of 7 Gly residues (7G-DkTx), and observed a Kx value that is indistinguishable from wild-type DkTx ([4.4 ± 0.03] × 106, Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is based on tryptophan fluorescence spectroscopy data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The suboptimal membrane partitioning of DkTx probably owes to direct interactions between the two lobes, possibly mediated through the same amphipathic surfaces that interact with the membrane.
source: This result seems to rule out the possibility that the linker restricts the dynamics of the two lobes significantly. Therefore, we deduce that the suboptimal membrane partitioning of DkTx probably owes to direct interactions between the two lobes, possibly mediated through the same amphipathic surfaces that interact with the membrane.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the 7G-DkTx partitioning data and the energetic penalty for bivalency.

claim: The most striking features of the cryo-EM structure of TRPV1 bound to DkTx, relative to the unbound structure, are the dilation of the outer pore within the selectivity filter (SF) region and the opening of the intracellular gate formed at the crossing between the S6 helices.
source: As noted previously (Cao et al., 2013), the most striking features of the cryo-EM structure of TRPV1 bound to DkTx, relative to the unbound structure, are the dilation of the outer pore within the selectivity filter (SF) region, and the opening of the intracellular gate that is formed at the crossing between the S6 helices.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the apo and DkTx-bound TRPV1 structures and supported by a citation to Cao et al., 2013.

claim: Binding of DkTx promotes changes in the transmembrane architecture of TRPV1 that pertain to the internal structure of each subunit and their relative arrangement.
source: This comparative analysis indicates that binding of DkTx promotes changes in the transmembrane architecture of the channel that pertain not only to the internal structure of each of the channel subunits, but also to their relative arrangement (Figure 6); as a result, these seemingly cooperative changes open up the constrictions observed in the apo structure, both in the SF region and the intracellular gate.
evidence: The claim is based on structural comparison of apo and DkTx-bound TRPV1 shown in Figure 6.

claim: The structural changes upon DkTx binding appear to be effected through displacements in the pore helix (P) and S6 helices relative to the S1-S4 unit and the transmembrane S5 segment.
source: These structural changes appear to be effected through displacements in the pore helix (P) and S6 helices relative to the S1-S4 unit and the transmembrane S5 segment; individually, the S1-S5 and P-S6 units are largely unchanged (RMSD ~ 0.7–0.8 Å) (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: The claim is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: The P and S6 helices become displaced relative to S1-S5 upon DkTx binding.
source: That the P and S6 helices become displaced relative to S1-S5 (Figure 6D) is consistent with the fact that their respective N-termini are the primary contacts for the toxin on the channel extracellular surface, as discussed above.
evidence: The claim is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 6D and is consistent with the toxin-channel contact analysis.

claim: The changes in P and S6 within a given subunit correlate with a pronounced rearrangement of the SF and pore loop in that same subunit.
source: The changes in P and S6 within a given subunit correlate very clearly with a pronounced rearrangement of the SF and pore loop in that same subunit (Figure 6D), but also with changes in the intracellular side of the channel.
evidence: The claim is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Displacements in the P and S6 helices are propagated to adjacent subunits and compounded to changes in their own internal structure.
source: The rationale for this remote effect is that the P and S6 helices are the main interfacial elements between adjacent subunits in the transmembrane domain of the channel (Figure 6E); therefore, displacements in these elements are propagated to the adjacent subunits, and compounded to the changes in their own internal structure.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The S1-S4 units become noticeably displaced relative to each other upon DkTx binding, affecting the crossing angle of helices S5 and S6 and the degree of opening of the intracellular gate.
source: As a result, the S1-S4 units (which as mentioned remain largely unchanged) become noticeably displaced relative to each other, thus affecting the crossing angle of helices S5 and S6, and hence the degree of opening of the intracellular gate (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The structural changes in the main-chain of TRPV1 upon DkTx binding correlate with the disruption of a cluster of hydrophobic interactions behind the SF.
source: Interestingly, the structural changes in the main-chain of the channel that are observed upon DkTx binding correlate with the disruption of a cluster of hydrophobic interactions behind the SF, at the interface between S5, the pore helix and S6, in close proximity to the contact region with the toxin (Figure 6G,H; Video 3).
evidence: The claim is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 6G,H and Video 3.

claim: The hydrophobic cluster behind the SF involves residues I599, F659, V595, F649, and T650.
source: This network involves, among others, residues I599, F659 and V595, F649, as well as T650.
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis of the hydrophobic cluster.

claim: Mutation of I599, F649, F659, V595, or T650 diminishes toxin-induced opening of TRPV1.
source: Only the latter two residues are nearby DkTx in the toxin-bound structure; however, mutation of any of these five residues diminishes toxin-induced opening of the channel, particularly in the case of I599A, F649A and F659A (Bohlen et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bohlen et al., 2010, which reported the mutagenesis results.

claim: There is a generalized reduction of contacts in the hydrophobic cluster in DkTx-bound TRPV1 relative to apo TRPV1.
source: When the degree of compactness of this hydrophobic network is quantified in terms of the number and persistence of pairwise side-chain contacts, it is apparent that there is a generalized reduction of these contacts in DkTx-bound TRPV1, relative to apo TRPV1 (Figure 6I).
evidence: The claim is based on MD simulation analysis shown in Figure 6I.

claim: M25 in K1 and L65 in K2 are two of the residues nearest to the hydrophobic cluster behind the SF and make frequent contact with channel residues in MD simulations.
source: In DkTx, two of the residues nearest to this hydrophobic cluster are M25 in K1 and L65 in K2, a relatively conserved position on the two knots that makes frequent contact with channel residues in the MD simulations (Figure 4D and Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is based on MD simulation analysis shown in Figure 4D and Figure 6G.

claim: M25 and L65 are predicted to play energetically important roles based on computational alanine-scanning of the toxin-channel interface.
source: Accordingly, both M25 and L65 are predicted to play energetically important roles based on our computational alanine-scan of the toxin-channel interface (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on computational alanine-scanning analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The L65A mutant of K2 dramatically reduced activation of TRPV1 and increased the rate of dissociation.
source: Although we have not yet tested other toxin residues that make direct contact with TRPV1 (such as W11/W53 and K14/K56), we mutated L65 in K2 to Ala and measured the concentration-dependence for activation of TRPV1 relative to wild-type K2. The L65A mutant dramatically reduced activation of K2 and increased the rate of dissociation (Figure 7A,B), confirming this residue mediates important interactions with the outer pore of TRPV1.
evidence: The claim is supported by functional data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: DkTx interacts with TRPV1 within the lipid membrane.
source: Our results demonstrate that DkTx interacts intimately with TRPV1 while inserting hydrophobic residues into the surrounding lipid membrane, and provide the first example of a complex structure between toxin and channel within a membrane environment.
evidence: The claim is based on the structural model and MD simulations showing concurrent toxin-channel and toxin-lipid interactions.

claim: The study provides the first example of a complex structure between toxin and channel within a membrane environment.
source: Our results demonstrate that DkTx interacts intimately with TRPV1 while inserting hydrophobic residues into the surrounding lipid membrane, and provide the first example of a complex structure between toxin and channel within a membrane environment.
evidence: The claim is based on the novelty of the structural findings in the context of toxin-channel interactions.

claim: DkTx uses a limited protein-protein interface to bind TRPV1.
source: Although the bivalency of DkTx clearly helps to prolong the lifetime of the toxin-channel complex (Bohlen et al., 2010), each lobe has relatively small protein-protein interfaces with TRPV1 (655 Å2 for K1 and 556 Å2 for K2), suggesting that the interaction of the toxin with the surrounding membrane is important for stabilizing the toxin-channel complex.
evidence: The claim is based on the calculated protein-protein interface areas from the structural model.

claim: The interaction of DkTx with the surrounding membrane is important for stabilizing the toxin-channel complex.
source: Although the bivalency of DkTx clearly helps to prolong the lifetime of the toxin-channel complex (Bohlen et al., 2010), each lobe has relatively small protein-protein interfaces with TRPV1 (655 Å2 for K1 and 556 Å2 for K2), suggesting that the interaction of the toxin with the surrounding membrane is important for stabilizing the toxin-channel complex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the small protein-protein interface and the observed toxin-lipid interactions.

claim: DkTx, PcTx1, and voltage-sensor toxins like hanatoxin and GxTx-1E adopt similar folds and display amphipathic surfaces that enable interactions with lipid membranes.
source: DkTx, PcTx1 and voltage-sensor toxins like hanatoxin and GxTx-1E adopt similar folds, and display amphipathic surfaces that enable interactions with lipid membranes (Figure 8) (Gupta et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 8 and supported by a citation to Gupta et al., 2015.

claim: In DkTx, residues in loops 2 and 4 engage the outer pore of TRPV1 while interacting with lipids in the surrounding membrane.
source: In DkTx, residues in loops 2 and 4 engage the outer pore of TRPV1, while interacting with lipids in the surrounding membrane (Figures 3, 4, 8A,B), and contain mostly hydrophobic residues (compare Figure 8A,B with Figure 1C,D where the toxins are oriented identically).
evidence: The claim is based on the structural model and MD simulations shown in Figures 3, 4, and 8A,B.

claim: In PcTx1, residues in loops 1 and 4 form a clamp-like structure for the toxin to bind to helix-5 within the extracellular thumb domain of the ASIC channel.
source: In PcTx1, residues in loops 1 and 4 form a clamp-like structure for the toxin to bind to helix-5 within the extracellular thumb domain of the ASIC channel (Figure 8D) (Baconguis and Gouaux, 2012; Dawson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Baconguis and Gouaux, 2012 and Dawson et al., 2012, and shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The voltage-sensor toxin GxTx-1E employs residues in loops 1 and 4 to bind to the S3b helix within the voltage-sensing domain of Kv channels.
source: Interestingly, the voltage-sensor toxin GxTx-1E also employs residues in loops 1 and 4 to bind to the S3b helix within the voltage-sensing domain of Kv channels, and these form a surface that resembles the one used by PcTx1 to bind to ASIC (Figure 8E) (Gupta et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gupta et al., 2015 and shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The common fold of tarantula toxins provides at least two distinct surfaces for engaging with ion channel proteins while maintaining favorable interactions with the lipid membrane.
source: Overall, this comparison suggests that the common fold of all these toxins provides at least two distinct surfaces for engaging with ion channel proteins, while maintaining favorable interactions with the lipid membrane.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural comparison of DkTx, PcTx1, and GxTx-1E.

claim: K2 is a more effective activator of TRPV1 when compared to K1.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that the K2 lobe is a more effective activator of TRPV1 when compared to K1 (see also Figure 3F), and that tethering of the two lobes of DkTx dramatically enhances the lifetime of the toxin-channel complex (Bae et al., 2012; Bohlen et al., 2010), similar to the avidity effect of a bivalent antibody.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bae et al., 2012 and Bohlen et al., 2010, and by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Tethering of the two lobes of DkTx dramatically enhances the lifetime of the toxin-channel complex.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that the K2 lobe is a more effective activator of TRPV1 when compared to K1 (see also Figure 3F), and that tethering of the two lobes of DkTx dramatically enhances the lifetime of the toxin-channel complex (Bae et al., 2012; Bohlen et al., 2010), similar to the avidity effect of a bivalent antibody.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bae et al., 2012 and Bohlen et al., 2010.

claim: The two lobes of DkTx have very different energetics for partitioning into lipid membranes, with K1 displaying considerably stronger interactions when compared to K2.
source: We find that the two lobes of DkTx also have very different energetics for partitioning into lipid membranes, with the K1 lobe displaying considerably stronger interactions when compared to K2, a trend that can be recapitulated in the bivalent K1K1 construct when compared to the bivalent K2K2 construct (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is based on tryptophan fluorescence spectroscopy data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Differences in binding affinity can explain why K2 is a much better activator of TRPV1 compared to K1.
source: Using bivalent K1K1 and K2K2 constructs, we also found that differences in binding affinity can explain why K2 is a much better activator of TRPV1 compared to K1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is based on functional data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Bivalency enables the two lobes of DkTx to be separately tuned for optimal membrane partitioning or affinity for binding to the channel.
source: Thus, bivalency not only increases the lifetime of the toxin-channel complex, but also enables the two lobes to be separately tuned for optimal membrane partitioning or affinity for binding to the channel.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential membrane partitioning and channel binding properties of K1 and K2.

claim: DkTx preferentially uses the K1 lobe to interact with membranes and thus raise the local concentration of K2 at the membrane surface, thereby promoting the initial formation of the toxin-channel complex using K2 within the interfacial region of the membrane.
source: This feature of DkTx would suggest that the toxin preferentially uses the K1 lobe to interact with membranes and thus raise the local concentration of K2 at the membrane surface, thereby promoting the initial formation of the toxin-channel complex using K2 within the interfacial region of the membrane (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is a proposed model shown in Figure 9 based on the differential properties of K1 and K2.

claim: The disruption of the hydrophobic cluster behind the SF leads to the structural changes required for ion permeation.
source: It is tantalizing to speculate that the disruption of this cluster, which implies an increased solvent exposure of more than a dozen hydrophobic side-chains across four channel subunits, leads not only to the structural changes required for ion permeation, but also to the kind of increase in the heat capacity of the protein that has been postulated to explain temperature sensing in TRP channels, including TRPV1 (Clapham and Miller, 2011).
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on the structural changes observed in the hydrophobic cluster.

claim: The disruption of the hydrophobic cluster behind the SF may lead to an increase in the heat capacity of TRPV1 that has been postulated to explain temperature sensing.
source: It is tantalizing to speculate that the disruption of this cluster, which implies an increased solvent exposure of more than a dozen hydrophobic side-chains across four channel subunits, leads not only to the structural changes required for ion permeation, but also to the kind of increase in the heat capacity of the protein that has been postulated to explain temperature sensing in TRP channels, including TRPV1 (Clapham and Miller, 2011).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by a citation to Clapham and Miller, 2011.

claim: Mutations at positions T633, F640 and Y653 within the hydrophobic cluster alter temperature sensitivity of TRPV1 without affecting activation by capsaicin.
source: Notably, mutations at positions T633, F640 and Y653 within the hydrophobic cluster have been shown to alter temperature sensitivity of the TRPV1 channel without affecting activation of the channel by capsaicin (Grandl et al., 2010; Myers et al., 2008; Ryu et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Grandl et al., 2010, Myers et al., 2008, and Ryu et al., 2007.

claim: An external Na+ binding site in the outer pore of TRPV1 tightly regulates temperature-sensor activation.
source: In addition, it is interesting that an external Na+ binding site in the outer pore of TRPV1 has been shown to tightly regulate temperature-sensor activation, and that DkTx renders TRPV1 temperature-insensitive over a wide temperature range (Jara-Oseguera, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jara-Oseguera, 2016.

claim: DkTx renders TRPV1 temperature-insensitive over a wide temperature range.
source: In addition, it is interesting that an external Na+ binding site in the outer pore of TRPV1 has been shown to tightly regulate temperature-sensor activation, and that DkTx renders TRPV1 temperature-insensitive over a wide temperature range (Jara-Oseguera, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jara-Oseguera, 2016.
